title: One front door for every model

beats.say: Twelve teams, three AI providers, and nobody knows who spent forty thousand dollars last weekend. Sound familiar?
Think of a hotel. Guests do not each get a key to the kitchen. They call the front desk, which knows who they are, what they may order, and keeps the bill.

chip.text: One bill, one set of rules

beats.say: An LLM gateway is that desk. Every team calls it instead of the providers. It holds the secret keys, checks each team's budget, and writes down what every call cost.
And when one kitchen closes, the desk sends the order to another, so the guest still eats.

check.q: Why put a gateway in front of AI models?
opts: One place for keys, budgets, fallbacks and cost records
It makes every model answer more accurately
It lets each team pick its own secret keys
check.why: The gateway handles the rules every team needs once, instead of twelve copies in twelve codebases.

work: List every service that calls a model provider directly today.
Find out who would notice if one team spent ten times its usual amount.

title: First token, then the rest

beats.say: Why does an AI answer start after a pause, then stream quickly? Two different phases.
First, prefill. The server reads your whole prompt at once, in parallel. A three thousand token prompt takes a few hundred milliseconds. That wait is the time to first token.
Then decode. Each new token needs a full pass that reads every weight from memory. At fifty tokens a second, a three hundred token answer takes six more seconds.
So stream the answer. The user feels only the first token, and shorter prompts and caching shrink that wait.

check.q: What mostly sets the time to first token?
opts: Queueing and prefill of the prompt
The number of output tokens
The temperature setting
check.why: The first token waits for the whole prompt to be processed; output length sets the time after that.

work: Measure p95 time to first token for one AI feature.
Check whether the feature streams its answers.

title: What one request costs

beats.say: A support assistant gets two hundred thousand requests a day. What does that cost? Let us do the sum.

Three thousand input tokens at three dollars a million is nine tenths of a cent. Three hundred output tokens at fifteen dollars a million is under half a cent. Together, about one point three five cents.
Cache the fixed two thousand token prefix and it drops to about eight tenths of a cent. Route seven in ten easy requests to a small model and the day falls to about six hundred forty dollars.
Every lever needs an eval run before and after, because cheaper answers can quietly be worse answers.

check.q: Which change lowers cost without touching answer quality, if done right?
opts: Caching a stable prompt prefix
Routing to a smaller model
Cutting the retrieved context in half
check.why: A cached prefix is the same text processed once; routing and trimming context can both change answers.

work: Work out cost per request for one feature you know.
Move the fixed part of a prompt to the start so it can be cached.

title: The KV cache and long context

beats.say: Why does a long conversation cost so much more than a short one? Memory.
While writing, the model keeps keys and values for every earlier token, in every layer, in GPU memory. For a seventy billion parameter model, that is about a third of a megabyte per token.
A thirty two thousand token conversation holds about ten gigabytes. Fewer conversations fit on a GPU, so throughput falls and the price rises.

show.title: GB of KV cache per conversation

beats.say: That is why retrieving the right three thousand tokens usually beats pasting in a hundred thousand.

check.q: Why does long context reduce how many users a GPU can serve?
opts: Its KV cache takes GPU memory per token
The model weights grow with each prompt
Long prompts need a larger model
check.why: The weights are fixed; the cache grows with every token in flight and crowds out other requests.

work: Check the average prompt length of your heaviest feature.
Try trimming retrieved context and rerun the eval set.

title: Batching, quantization and their trade-offs

beats.say: One GPU, one user, one token at a time? That wastes almost all of it.
Each decode step reads all the weights. Reading them once for fifty users costs nearly the same as for one. Continuous batching adds and removes requests at every step.
The catch: each user sees slightly slower tokens, and a full server queues new requests. Operators cap the batch size to hold a latency target.
Quantization stores weights in eight or four bits. Less to read means faster and cheaper, but check quality on your own eval set, never a leaderboard.

check.q: What does continuous batching trade away for higher throughput?
opts: A little speed for each user
Answer accuracy
Prompt caching
check.why: Sharing each weight read across many requests raises throughput, while each request decodes a bit slower.

work: Ask your serving team what batch size limit they run.
Compare a quantized model with the original on your eval set.

title: Retries, fallbacks and budgets

beats.say: The provider says too many requests. Should you retry? Once.
A rate limit is often brief, so one retry with a short wait is fair. Retrying forever turns a hiccup into a storm and a bill.

show.title: Retry rules
items: One retry on a rate limit

beats.say: On an outage or timeout, the gateway falls back to another model that has passed the same evals. An untested fallback just fails differently.
And a daily budget per team, with an alert at eighty percent, catches the agent stuck in a loop before the weekend does.

check.q: A provider has an outage. What should the gateway do?
opts: Fall back to a model that passed the same evals
Retry the same call until it works
Return an error to every user at once
check.why: A tested fallback keeps the feature up; endless retries add load and cost.

work: Check whether your fallback model was ever run against your eval set.
Set a per-team daily budget alert.

title: Gateway or not, API or self-host?

beats.say: Does every company need an LLM gateway and its own GPUs? No.
One team, one model, a small bill: a client library with retries is enough. A gateway pays off when many teams share providers, budgets and data rules.
Use an API until something forces a change: high steady volume where busy GPUs are cheaper, data that cannot leave your network, or a fine-tuned open model.

chip.text: Move only for volume or data rules

beats.say: Self-hosting means owning GPU capacity, batching, quantization choices, upgrades and the pager. Price the people, not just the GPUs.

check.q: Which is the strongest reason to self-host a model?
opts: Data that may not leave your own network
Wanting a faster first prototype
A team of two calling one model
check.why: Data residency is a hard requirement; the other two are better served by an API.

work: Write down which of your AI data may not leave your network.
Estimate GPU cost against your current API bill at steady volume.

title: Owning the gateway, and how it fails

beats.say: Who owns the gateway, and who owns the prompts? Get this wrong and it becomes a bottleneck.
A platform team owns the gateway, provider contracts, quotas and the eval gate for new models. Feature teams own their prompts, eval sets and quality.
It fails as provider outages, timeouts on long prompts, cost spikes from loops, quiet quality drops after a model update, and a gateway that adds latency or goes down itself.

show.title: Watch for
items: The gateway as a single point

beats.say: Move off it when the provider's own gateway covers every model you use, or when one feature's volume earns dedicated serving.

show.title: Move off when
items: One feature needs its own path

check.q: Which should stay with the feature team, not the gateway?
opts: The prompt and its eval set
Quotas and budgets
Provider keys
check.why: Cross-cutting rules live in the gateway; a gateway that edits prompts becomes everyone's bottleneck.

work: Decide who approves a new model before any team can use it.
Make cost per feature visible to each team monthly.
Add a health check and a second instance for the gateway.

title: From demo to restaurant

beats.say: Why does an AI chatbot that wowed everyone in the demo fall apart in real life?

Cooking one great dinner for friends is a demo. Running a restaurant is production. Now you serve a million meals a day to strangers, on a budget, and someone gets a phone call at night if the kitchen catches fire.

show.title: A demo is a dinner, production is a *restaurant*

beats.say: The AI model is just the chef. A restaurant also needs a front door that checks who comes in, a way to avoid cooking the same dish twice, and someone tasting plates to check quality.

chip.text: Everything around the chef is the job

beats.say: Four things decide if it survives: are the answers right, how fast do they arrive, what does each plate cost, and is it safe.

show.title: Four numbers decide survival
items: Safety: what it may touch or say

check.q: In the restaurant picture, what does the AI model represent?
opts: One part of the kitchen, with doors, checks and costs around it
The whole restaurant, since the model does all the work
The customers, because they send in the requests
The menu, which is written once and never changes
check.why: The model is one component, the chef. Production work is everything around it: access control, caching, quality checks, cost and safety.

work: List the four things around the model in your own AI feature: quality, latency, cost, safety.
Ask who gets paged if your AI feature breaks tonight.
Write down one thing the demo never had to handle.

title: Where the time goes

beats.say: Where does the time go when someone presses enter on an AI feature?
The app sends the request to a gateway. The gateway checks keys and quotas, then looks in a cache. On a hit, the answer returns in milliseconds and costs nothing.
On a miss, the model reads your whole prompt at once. That is called prefill. Then it writes one token at a time, called decode. A token is roughly three quarters of a word.
Say prefill takes 400 milliseconds and decode runs at 50 tokens a second. A 500 token answer takes about ten seconds in total. But streaming shows the first words in under a second.

check.q: Why does streaming make a ten second answer feel faster?
opts: The first words appear after prefill, so the user starts reading early
The model finishes decoding sooner when it streams its output
The gateway skips the cache check when it streams tokens
Streaming cuts the number of tokens in every answer
check.why: Total time is unchanged. Streaming shows tokens as they are decoded, so the wait for something to see is roughly just prefill.

work: Measure time to first token and total time separately for your feature.
Check your cache hit rate and what a hit saves per request.
Add a trace span for each step: gateway, cache, prefill, decode.

title: Averages hide the pain

beats.say: Your average latency is two seconds, so why are users complaining?
Averages hide the slow tail. The 95th percentile is the time that one request in twenty is slower than. If one user action makes five model calls, nearly one user in four hits at least one slow call.
Cost hides the same way. Three cents a request sounds tiny. At a million requests a day, that is thirty thousand dollars a day. Retries and long prompts multiply it.
And failures are quiet. A model can return a fluent wrong answer with no error code. So you need evals and traces, not just uptime checks.

show.title: Quiet failures
items: Uptime checks see none of it

check.q: A feature has a good average latency but angry users. What is the best first move?
opts: Look at p95 latency and trace the slowest requests
Trust the average, since most requests are fast
Add more retries so slow calls get another chance
Switch to a larger model so answers are better
check.why: Averages hide the slow tail. Percentiles and traces show which requests are slow and which step is responsible. Blind retries can add load and cost.

work: Put p95 and p99 latency on the dashboard, not only the average.
Compute dollars per request and per day, including retries.
Sample live answers weekly and score them against your eval set.

title: What guards are worth

beats.say: When should you not build your own gateway, evals and tracing stack?

Every guard adds a hop and some milliseconds. A gateway, a cache and a redaction step each earn their place only if they save more than they cost. For one small internal tool, a direct API call with logging is enough.

chip.text: Add layers as scale and risk grow

beats.say: Scale changes the maths. At a million requests a day, a ten percent cache hit rate, or a cheaper model for easy questions, can save thousands of dollars daily. Route by difficulty, and fall back to a second provider when the first is down.
Set a budget for quality, latency, cost and safety before launch. Then you can say which one you will trade away, instead of discovering it during an outage.

show.title: Decide trade-offs up front
items: Quality target on an eval set
Safety limits on read and write

check.q: When is a full gateway with caching and redaction most justified?
opts: High volume or sensitive data, where savings and safety outweigh added hops
Any feature at all, since extra layers never add cost
Only demos, because they are the least predictable
Only when the model is small and the prompts are short
check.why: Each layer adds latency and upkeep. It pays off when volume makes savings large or when data and actions need central control.

work: Write a one page budget for quality, latency, cost and safety for each AI feature.
Estimate savings from caching and model routing before building either.
Name a fallback provider and test the switch before you need it.

title: Read fast, write slow

beats.say: Why does a chatbot pause, then type out its answer slowly?

show.sub: Two different jobs are hiding here

beats.say: It works in two phases. First it reads your whole question at once, like taking in a page at a glance. That is fast, because many words are handled side by side. This phase is called prefill.

Then it writes the answer one word at a time. For every single word, it must fetch its whole giant reference book from storage. The fetching is the slow part, not the thinking. This phase is called decode.
The wait before the first word is what you feel as, is it working? Streaming shows each word as it is ready, so the wait feels short.

show.title: What the user feels
items: The wait before the first word is the one that matters
Streaming shows words as they are ready
The full answer still takes the same time

check.q: Why is writing an answer word by word slower than reading the question?
opts: Each new word needs the whole model fetched from memory again
The model reads the question twice before it starts writing
Words in the answer are harder to spell than words in the question
The question is shorter, so it always finishes sooner
check.why: Reading handles many words side by side. Writing needs a full pass through the model for every word, and each pass is held back by fetching the model's weights from memory.

work: Open your chat feature and note when the first word appears versus when the last one does.
Check that every user-facing chat call has streaming switched on.
Explain prefill and decode to a teammate using the reading and writing picture.

title: Prefill, decode and the two clocks

beats.say: A 3,000 token prompt, and a 300 token answer. Where do the seconds go?

Prefill reads all 3,000 input tokens in parallel. That is limited by compute, so it takes only a few hundred milliseconds. Add queueing and network, and you get time to first token, the moment the user sees something.

Decode is different. Each new token needs a pass through the whole model, and each pass reads every weight from GPU memory. Memory bandwidth is the limit. At 50 tokens a second, 300 tokens take 6 seconds.
That is also why output tokens cost more than input tokens. Stream them, and the user waits for the first token, not the last.

check.q: A request has a 3,000 token prompt and a 300 token answer, streamed. What sets how long the user waits to see anything?
opts: Queueing, network and prefill of the prompt
Decode speed multiplied by the answer length
The size of the answer the model plans to give
The memory bandwidth used while writing the answer
check.why: Streaming means the user sees output once the first token arrives. That is queueing plus network plus prefill. Decode speed only controls how fast the rest follows.

work: Log time to first token and tokens per second as two separate metrics.
Estimate answer time for your top feature as output tokens divided by decode speed.
Set a maximum output length on every call so decode time has a ceiling.

title: Why the average lies

beats.say: Your average latency looks fine, yet users complain. Why?

show.text: Fine on average, slow for users

beats.say: The mean hides the slow tail. Long prompts, busy servers and retries all land there. So budget with the 95th percentile, the time that 95 out of 100 requests beat.

show.title: Budget with p95
items: The mean hides the slow tail
Long prompts, busy servers, retries land in the tail
p95: 95 of 100 requests are faster than this

beats.say: Then add up the steps. Gateway, 20 milliseconds. Retrieval and reranking, 250. Queue and prefill, 600. That keeps time to first token under one second.
Decode is separate. 300 tokens at 50 a second is 6 seconds, but it streams, so it feels fine. A longer prompt blows time to first token. A longer answer blows total time.

chip.text: Each cost hits a different budget

check.q: Why should a latency budget use the 95th percentile instead of the mean?
opts: The mean hides slow requests from long prompts, busy servers and retries
The mean is hard to compute across many servers
The 95th percentile is always the fastest number to hit
The mean only counts the decode phase and ignores prefill
check.why: A few slow requests barely move the mean, yet those are the ones users notice. The 95th percentile shows what the slow tail looks like.

work: Chart p50 and p95 time to first token for each feature, not only the average.
Write a per-step p95 budget and compare it to what traces show.
Alert when the p95 prompt length grows, since it eats the prefill budget.

title: Pulling the right latency lever

beats.say: The budget is blown. Which lever do you pull first?

show.sub: Pick the lever that fits the cause

beats.say: Cut prefill. Shorten the prompt, or use prompt caching so a repeated prefix is not reprocessed. Cut decode. Ask for brevity and set a maximum output length, since every output token is slow and costs more.

show.title: Cut the work
items: Prompt caching skips a repeated prefix
Brevity and a max length cut slow, costly output tokens

beats.say: Or change the model or the place. A smaller model decodes faster but may answer worse. A closer region trims network time but may limit your choices.

The best lever is often no wait at all. Precompute summaries in batch, before the user asks. Use that when questions are predictable. Skip it when inputs are unique, because you pay for work nobody reads.

check.q: When is precomputing summaries in batch a poor choice?
opts: When inputs are unique, so most precomputed work is never read
When users ask the same predictable questions every day
When a fast answer matters more than the freshest data
When the summaries can be stored and served from a cache
check.why: Precomputing trades spend for speed. It pays off when many users want the same predictable output. With unique inputs you pay for summaries nobody reads.

work: Rank your slowest features by whether prefill, decode or retrieval dominates, then pick one lever for each.
Turn on prompt caching for any prompt with a large stable prefix.
List which features have predictable inputs and could be precomputed in batch.

title: Why talking costs more than listening

beats.say: Why does a long answer cost more than a long question?
Imagine a consultant who bills by the word. Reading your brief is quick and cheap. Writing the reply is slow, careful work, so each word they write costs several times more.
Now say you hand them the same thick rulebook every morning. Reading it fresh each time wastes money. So they keep a copy in a drawer, and charge you a small fee to glance at it.

chip.text: Repeated text is billed at a discount

beats.say: AI models work the same way. They charge by the token, which is a small chunk of a word. Output tokens cost the most, and repeated text kept in the drawer costs the least.

check.q: In the consultant story, why is keeping the rulebook in a drawer cheaper?
opts: Reading the same text again is billed at a small discount
The consultant writes shorter replies when a rulebook exists
The rulebook turns every reply into a cheaper kind of word
Words in the rulebook are free once the first day has passed
check.why: Cached input is the repeated text. Providers charge much less for it than for fresh input, though it is not free and it still costs something.

work: List which parts of your prompts are identical on every request.
Find the price list for your model and note input, output and cached rates.
Ask your team who currently sees the token bill.

title: Working out one request

beats.say: What does one support chat actually cost? Let's do the sums.

Prices are three dollars per million input tokens and fifteen per million output. Input costs nine thousandths of a dollar. Output costs four and a half thousandths. That is one point three five cents a request, or two thousand seven hundred dollars a day.

chip.text: Output is 9% of tokens, a third of cost

beats.say: Two thousand input tokens are the same system prompt every time. Cache them at thirty cents per million and a request falls to eighty-one hundredths of a cent. That is sixteen hundred twenty dollars a day.
Now answer seventy percent of requests with a small model, at a quarter dollar in and one twenty-five out. The bill drops to about six hundred forty dollars a day.

check.q: With 3,000 input and 300 output tokens, why is output still a big share of the bill?
opts: Each output token is priced about five times an input token
Output tokens are counted twice, once when made and when read
Output is billed per request while input is billed per token
Output tokens cannot be cached, so they use the cached rate
check.why: At fifteen dollars against three per million, 300 output tokens cost $0.0045, a third of the request even though they are under a tenth of the tokens.

work: Write the cost per request for your top three prompts using real token counts.
Multiply by daily volume to get a figure for the first design review question.
Measure what share of your spend is output tokens.

title: Why the cache stopped saving money

beats.say: Why did our cached prompt suddenly stop saving money?

show.text: Cache hit rate fell to zero
show.sub: nothing in the prompt looked wrong

beats.say: A cache matches the prompt from the very first token. If you put the current time or the user's name at the top, every request looks new, and the stored prefix is never reused. Stable text goes first. The question goes last.

chip.text: Move changing text to the end

beats.say: Caches also expire after minutes of silence, and very short prefixes may not qualify. Writing to the cache can cost a little extra, so a prefix used only once is a loss.

show.title: Cache limits
items: A prefix used once loses money

beats.say: Watch hidden output as well. Reasoning tokens and retries are billed as output, the dearest kind. Cap output length, and log tokens for every request.

chip.text: Log input, cached and output tokens

check.q: A team adds the current date to the top of a long cached system prompt. What happens?
opts: Every request differs early on, so the prefix is not reused
Only the date tokens are recomputed and the rest is reused
The cache keeps working but charges the full input rate
Dates are ignored by the cache because they are short text
check.why: Prefix caching needs an exact match from the first token. A changing value near the top makes each prompt different, so nothing stored can be reused.

work: Move timestamps, user names and retrieved documents below the fixed instructions.
Track cache hit rate per prompt and alert when it drops.
Set a maximum output length and count retries in cost reports.

title: Does the feature pay for itself?

beats.say: The bill is falling, but is the feature paying for itself?

show.text: Monthly bill or cost per resolution?
show.sub: leadership sees one, you need the other

beats.say: Track cost per resolved conversation, not the monthly bill. A cheap answer that fails sends the customer to a human agent, who costs far more. Savings that cut the resolution rate can lose money.

chip.text: A failed cheap answer is not cheap

beats.say: Routing seventy percent to a small model saved about a thousand dollars a day here. But it needs a router and quality tests. At a few thousand requests a day, the engineering time may cost more than it saves.

show.title: Routing trade-offs
items: Saves about $1,000 a day at 200,000 requests
Needs a router and quality tests
Small volume may not repay the effort

beats.say: Send anything that can wait, like yesterday's tickets, to a batch interface for roughly half price. Keep live chat on the fast path.

check.q: A new setup halves the cost per request but resolves fewer chats. What should you check?
opts: Cost per resolved conversation, including human handoffs
Total tokens per day, since lower tokens always means savings
Average latency, because speed decides if a feature pays off
Monthly bill alone, because it is what leadership reviews
check.why: Cheap requests that fail push work to human agents. Only cost per resolved conversation shows whether the feature really pays for itself.

work: Add resolution rate and human handoff cost to the cost dashboard.
Run quality evals on a small model before routing any traffic to it.
Move offline jobs, such as ticket classification, to a batch API.

title: The bus that shares its fuel

beats.say: Why does a busy chatbot server cost less per person than a quiet one?

Picture a bus. Driving it across town costs the same whether it carries one rider or forty. A model server works the same way. For every word it writes, the GPU must read the whole model from memory. That read is the fuel.

chip.text: Each word costs one full read

beats.say: Serve one user and you pay for the whole trip for one rider. Serve forty together and each pays a fortieth. Modern servers even let riders hop on and off at every stop, so seats never sit empty.

chip.text: Riders hop on and off every stop

check.q: Why is a model server cheaper per user when many users are served together?
opts: Reading the model from memory is shared across all the users in the batch
Each user's request gets a smaller copy of the model to run faster
The GPU skips the memory read when more than one user is waiting
check.why: Every token needs the weights read from memory. Batching shares that one read across many users, like riders sharing a bus trip.

work: Ask your platform team what share of GPU time is busy versus idle.
When you explain API pricing, use the bus idea: shared reads make busy capacity cheaper.

title: The notes that fill the desk

beats.say: Why does a very long chat make the server slower and pricier, even though the model is the same size?

show.text: Long chat, same model, higher bill?

beats.say: Think of a student writing an essay. After each sentence, rereading every earlier page would take forever. So she keeps short notes on each page. Those notes are the KV cache: the model's saved working for every word so far.

Notes make writing fast. But they take desk space, and every new word adds more. A long conversation fills the desk. A hundred chats at once fill it faster. The notes, not the model, are what run out of room.

check.q: In the notes analogy, why does a longer conversation cost the server more?
opts: The model itself grows larger as the chat gets longer
Saved notes for every word take more memory as the chat grows
The server must download the model again for each new word
check.why: The KV cache stores working for each earlier token, so it grows with conversation length. The model weights stay the same size.

work: Before launch, ask how long real conversations get, not just the average.
Trim chat history you do not need to send each turn.

title: Weights, bytes and quantization

beats.say: How much GPU memory does a seventy billion parameter model need before a single user shows up?

Memory is parameters times bytes per parameter. In sixteen-bit precision each parameter takes two bytes. Seventy billion times two is about one hundred forty gigabytes. One GPU holds eighty. So you need at least two.
Quantization stores each weight in fewer bits. Eight-bit halves it to seventy gigabytes. Four-bit quarters it to about thirty-five. Less to read means faster decode, and fewer GPUs.
The cost is a small quality loss. Measure it on your own eval set, not a public benchmark.

check.q: You move a model from 16-bit to 8-bit weights. What should you expect?
opts: Half the weight memory, so faster reads, and a quality change to measure
Half the weight memory, with output quality guaranteed identical
The same memory, but the model runs on a newer kind of GPU
check.why: 8-bit halves the bytes per weight, so less to store and read. Quality may shift slightly, so you test it on your own data.

work: Compute weights memory as parameters times bytes before choosing GPUs.
Run your eval set on the quantized model and compare scores.
Leave headroom beyond weights for the KV cache.

title: KV cache math

beats.say: Why does one long conversation hold ten gigabytes of GPU memory?
Each new token needs attention over every earlier token. Recomputing that each time is slow, so the server saves each token's keys and values in every layer. That saved data is the KV cache.
For a seventy billion model: two, for keys and values, times eighty layers, times eight heads, times one hundred twenty-eight size, times two bytes. About a third of a megabyte per token.

show.title: Bytes per token
show.text: 2 x 80 x 8 x 128 x 2 = about 0.33 MB
show.note: keys and values, layers, heads, head size, bytes

beats.say: Multiply by thirty-two thousand tokens and you get about ten gigabytes for one chat. Long contexts cost memory because of this cache, not because of the weights.

check.q: What mainly makes a 32,000-token conversation expensive to serve?
opts: The weights are copied again for every conversation
The KV cache holds saved keys and values for every token
Attention gets recomputed from scratch and stored as extra weights
check.why: The cache stores keys and values per token in every layer, about 0.33 MB per token here. Weights are shared across users.

work: Estimate KV cache per token for your model and multiply by your real context length.
Divide free GPU memory by per-chat cache to find how many chats fit.

title: Continuous batching and paged memory

beats.say: What goes wrong when a server waits for a whole batch to finish before starting new requests?

One long answer holds everyone hostage. Short requests finish, their GPU slots sit idle, and new users queue. Modern servers instead add and remove requests at every decode step, so slots refill immediately.
Memory has a trap too. Reserving one big block per request for its maximum length leaves gaps. So the KV cache is split into small fixed-size blocks, handed out as needed, like pages in a book.
Throughput rises several times. The trade-off: bigger batches give the server more tokens per second, but each user's tokens arrive slightly slower. Tune batch size against your latency target.

check.q: What is the main benefit of continuous batching over waiting for whole batches?
opts: Each user's tokens always arrive faster than before
Requests join and leave each step, so GPU slots stay busy
Memory use for the KV cache drops to nearly zero
check.why: Adding and removing requests at every decode step keeps the GPU full and raises throughput. Per-user speed can dip slightly as batches grow.

work: Load test at your real concurrency and watch both throughput and per-user latency.
Check that your server uses paged KV blocks and monitor cache utilisation.

title: Speculative decoding

beats.say: Can a model write several tokens for the price of one pass?
Decode is slow because each token needs a full read of the weights. Speculative decoding adds a small draft model that guesses, say, four tokens cheaply.
The large model then checks all four in one pass. Right guesses are kept, so several tokens arrive for one expensive read. At the first wrong guess, it discards the rest and uses its own token.
Output quality is the same, because the large model has the final say. The gain depends on how often the draft is right. On unpredictable text, you gain little and still pay for the draft's memory.

show.title: Caveats
items: Speedup depends on draft hit rate

check.q: Why does speculative decoding not lower output quality?
opts: The draft model is trained to match the large model exactly
The large model checks every guess and overrides the wrong ones
Wrong guesses are rare enough that nobody notices them
check.why: The large model verifies the draft's tokens and replaces the first wrong one with its own, so the result matches normal decoding.

work: Measure the draft acceptance rate on your real traffic before adopting it.
Budget GPU memory for the draft model too.

title: API or self-host?

beats.say: When is renting a model through an API cheaper than owning GPUs?
Almost always, at first. An API charges per token and you pay nothing when idle. Self-hosting means you pay for GPUs every hour, whether busy or not, plus upgrades, scaling and on-call.
Switch only when something forces it. Very high steady volume that keeps GPUs busy. Data that may not leave your network. Or a fine-tuned open model you need to run.

show.title: Valid reasons to self-host
items: High, steady volume keeps GPUs busy
You need a fine-tuned open model

beats.say: If one narrow task is the bulk of spend, distil a large model's answers into a small model, then serve that. Either way, quantize, batch and measure utilisation before buying more GPUs.

check.q: Your traffic is small and spiky, and data may leave your network. What do you choose?
opts: Self-host, because owning GPUs always beats per-token pricing
Self-host, because quantization removes the need for on-call
Use an API, because you pay only for tokens you actually use
check.why: With low or spiky volume, self-hosted GPUs sit idle and still cost money. An API charges only for use and avoids operating the fleet.

work: Model monthly cost for API versus GPUs at your expected utilisation, including staff time.
List which constraints force self-hosting: volume, data rules, fine-tuned models.
Find your single most expensive narrow task and test a distilled small model on it.

title: Cheaper AI is like a smart kitchen

beats.say: Why does one chatbot answer in a second for a penny, while another takes ten seconds and costs ten times more?

Think of a restaurant kitchen. Prep done before the rush is like caching. The chopped onions are ready, so every order starts faster. Prompt caching does this for the part of your question that never changes.
A good kitchen also gives simple orders to a junior cook and hard dishes to the head chef. That is routing: a small, cheap model for easy tasks, a big one for hard tasks.
But every shortcut can hurt. If the junior burns the toast, customers notice. So taste-test before and after each change. That test is called an eval.

show.sub: An eval checks answer quality before and after

check.q: Why must you run an eval before and after making an AI system cheaper?
opts: A cheaper setup can quietly give worse answers
Cheaper setups always break the system outright
Evals are what make the model itself run faster
check.why: Savings levers can lower quality without any error showing up. Only measuring answers before and after reveals that.

work: List which parts of your prompts never change between calls.
Pick ten easy and ten hard real requests to compare models on.
Agree that no cost change ships without a quality check.

title: Prompt caching and shorter context

beats.say: Your app sends the same three thousand words of instructions on every single call. Why pay to process them every time?

Prompt caching stores the model's work on the start of your prompt. The next call with an identical start skips that work. Input cost drops, and the first word arrives sooner. That wait is time to first token.
The catch: the match must be exact from the first character. Put a timestamp at the top and every call looks new, so the cache never hits. Keep stable text first and changing text last.

show.title: Order matters
items: A timestamp on top breaks it

beats.say: Shorter context works differently. Retrieve five chunks instead of twenty, and the model reads fewer tokens before answering. That reading step is prefill. But drop the chunk holding the fact, and quality falls.

check.q: A team adds the current time as the first line of a long prompt. What happens to prompt caching?
opts: Every call has a new prefix, so hits stop
The cache still hits since the rest is identical
Only the first line gets recomputed each call
check.why: Caching matches the prompt from the first character. A changing first line makes every prefix different, so nothing is reused.

work: Move timestamps and user data to the end of your prompts.
Track cache hit rate per endpoint.
Test fewer retrieved chunks on an eval set before shipping.

title: Routing and cascades with real numbers

beats.say: If eighty percent of your requests are easy, why send them all to your biggest model?

show.sub: Yet all go to the biggest model

beats.say: Routing uses rules or a small classifier to pick a model per task. Reset a password goes to the small model. Analyse a contract goes to the large one. Small models can cost a tenth as much.
A cascade is different. Try the small model first. If it seems unsure, or a check fails, escalate to the large model.
Say small costs one and large costs ten. If eighty percent stay small, average cost is about three. But an escalated request pays for both calls and waits twice.

check.q: In a cascade, what is true of a request that gets escalated to the large model?
opts: It costs more than calling the large model alone
It costs the same as calling the large model alone
It costs less since the small model did some work
check.why: The escalated request pays for the failed small call plus the large call, and waits for both, so it is worse than going straight to large.

work: Measure what share of requests would stay on the small model.
Log escalation rate and its added latency.
Evaluate each route separately on its own examples.

title: Semantic caching: when similar is wrong

beats.say: A user asks to refund order 1041. Your cache returns the answer for order 1042. What went wrong?

Semantic caching stores past answers and reuses one when a new question is close in meaning, measured with embeddings. Close in meaning is not the same as the same answer. One digit changes everything.
Two more failures. Stale answers: the policy changed, but the cache still serves last month's. And leaks: one user's private answer shown to another user.

show.title: Failure modes
items: One user's answer shown to another

beats.say: So use it only for public, stable answers, like opening hours or product FAQs. Set an expiry, keep entries separate per tenant, and tune the similarity threshold on real questions.

check.q: Which request is the safest candidate for a semantic cache?
opts: What are your opening hours on public holidays
Refund the order I placed yesterday for me
Summarise the account balance for this customer
check.why: Public, stable, user-independent answers can be reused safely. Refunds and balances depend on the user and change over time.

work: Exclude anything with ids, amounts or personal data from the cache.
Add expiry and a per-tenant key.
Review a sample of cache hits for wrong reuse.

title: Why your prompt cache goes cold

beats.say: Your prompt cache worked yesterday. Today the bill doubled and the code did not change. Why?
Cache hits need an identical prefix. A request ID, today's date, or a shuffled list of tools near the top changes the prefix, so every call misses.

show.title: Silent prefix breakers
items: Today's date in the system text

beats.say: Entries also expire after a short idle time. With low traffic, the cache goes cold between calls, and you pay full price again.
Check cache hit rate in your traces. If it drops, diff the prompts. Keep static text first, dynamic text last, and treat any prompt edit as a change to test.

show.sub: A drop means the prefix changed

check.q: Cache hit rate falls sharply after a deploy that touched no model settings. What do you check first?
opts: Whether the start of the prompt now differs per call
Whether the model has become less accurate overall
Whether the provider raised the price of output
check.why: A hit needs an identical prefix. A new varying field near the top is the usual cause, and a prompt diff reveals it.

work: Alert on cache hit rate per endpoint.
Diff rendered prompts across two deploys.
Keep tool and example order fixed.

title: Choosing levers when the bill must halve

beats.say: You must cut the AI bill in half. Which lever do you pull first, and how do you know it is safe?
Start with the nearly free ones. Prompt caching and batch jobs cost almost no quality. Precompute answers overnight where you can. The trade is freshness.

Next, routing or a smaller distilled model. Each needs its own eval and upkeep as models change. Cascades pay off only if most requests stay small. Otherwise escalations cost more than calling the large model alone.
Whatever you pick, run the eval before and after. Every lever can quietly lower quality, and a cheaper wrong answer is not a saving.

check.q: Which order of levers is the best default for cutting cost with the least quality risk?
opts: Caching and batching first, then routing and smaller models
A distilled model first, then caching once quality is proven
Semantic caching first for every endpoint, then everything else
check.why: Caching an identical prefix and batching barely touch quality. Routing and smaller models carry quality risk and need per-route evals, so they come later.

work: Rank levers by savings and by quality risk before choosing.
Require an eval run before and after each change.
Re-check routes and distilled models when the base model changes.

title: The travel desk for AI models

beats.say: Three teams, three secret keys, three bills nobody can compare. How do you tame that?

Picture a company travel desk. Instead of everyone holding the company credit card and booking flights themselves, they ask the desk. The desk is the gateway. It sits in front of every AI model, the way a receptionist sits in front of every office.

show.title: One *desk* in front of every model

beats.say: The desk checks who you are, caps your spending, and if one airline cancels, books another that is just as good. It also keeps a receipt for every trip, so finance sees who spent what.

show.title: What the desk does
items: Rebooks if a flight is cancelled
Keeps a receipt for every trip

beats.say: But the desk never plans your trip. The prompt and the product stay with your team.

show.text: The desk never plans the trip
show.sub: Prompts and product stay with the feature team

check.q: In the travel desk analogy, what should the gateway NOT do?
opts: Decide what the prompt says and how the product behaves
Hold the provider keys instead of each team holding them
Switch to a backup model when the first one is down
Record which team spent how much on each call
check.why: The gateway handles keys, limits, fallbacks and receipts. The prompt and product logic belong to the team that owns the feature, otherwise the gateway becomes a bottleneck.

work: List every team that calls a model today and where each provider key lives.
Write down who currently pays for each model bill and whether anyone can see it per feature.

title: Following one request through a gateway

beats.say: A request hits the gateway. What happens in the next few milliseconds before any model sees it?

show.sub: What does the gateway do first?

beats.say: First it checks the team's key and quota, say one hundred thousand tokens a minute and fifty dollars a day. Then it strips personal data, like emails and phone numbers, so they never leave your network.

Then it calls the model with two timers: two seconds to the first token, thirty seconds in total. A rate limit error gets one retry after a short wait. An outage goes to a backup model that passed the same evals.

show.title: The call, with *timers* and a backup

beats.say: Finally it writes one trace: model, prompt version, tokens, cost, latency, and team. That is how cost shows up per feature.

check.q: Why does the gateway set a separate time-to-first-token timeout as well as a total timeout?
opts: It spots a stuck call within seconds instead of waiting out the full total
It lets the gateway cache the first token for later repeat requests
It makes the model produce its answer faster after it starts to stream
It splits the bill between the team and the provider for each call
check.why: A stuck call may never produce a token. A short first-token timer frees the user or worker quickly, while the total timer caps calls that stream too slowly.

work: Set a first-token timeout and a total timeout on every model call, and log when each fires.
Add team and prompt version tags to every call so cost can be grouped per feature.

title: Retry storms, bad fallbacks and cache order

beats.say: Why can a gateway's retry logic take down the very provider it is protecting?
If every call retries three times, a rate limit makes traffic triple, which causes more rate limits. That is a retry storm. So retry once with backoff, then fail or fall back. Never retry forever.
Fallback has a trap too. A backup model that was never evaluated may answer fast and wrong. Only fail over to models that passed the same evals.

chip.text: Only fail over to tested models

beats.say: Two more gotchas. Prompt caching only works when the stable part comes first, so put the system prompt before user text. And a time-to-first-token timeout catches stuck streams that a total timeout would miss for half a minute.

show.title: More gotchas
items: Stable prompt first, user text last
Total timeout alone waits too long

check.q: A provider starts returning rate limit errors. What is the safest gateway behavior?
opts: Retry once with backoff, then fall back or return an error
Retry every call until it succeeds so no request is ever lost
Retry instantly three times from every worker to clear the queue
Disable the quota for that team until the provider recovers
check.why: Unbounded or instant retries multiply traffic and deepen the rate limit. One backed-off retry, then a tested fallback or a clear error, keeps load bounded.

work: Cap retries at one with backoff, and alert when the retry rate climbs.
Run your eval set against every fallback model before adding it to the chain.
Check that prompts put the fixed system text before the changing user text.

title: When a gateway is worth it, and when it is not

beats.say: When is a gateway the wrong answer?
With one team and one model, it is extra moving parts. A direct call with good logging is cheaper. The gateway pays off around the third team, when keys, bills and retries start to diverge.

Once you adopt it, it sits on every request, so it is a single point of failure. Run several copies, keep it stateless, and it must stream without adding noticeable delay. Buy or build by three tests: supports every provider you use, streams cleanly, exports traces to your tools.
And keep it thin. If it starts rewriting prompts, every team waits on it. Own the policy, leave the product to the teams.

check.q: Which situation most clearly argues against adding an LLM gateway right now?
opts: One team calls one model, and a direct call with logging is enough
Three teams each hold their own keys and write their own retry code
Finance cannot see which feature drives most of the model bill
Personal data must be removed before requests reach any provider
check.why: A gateway adds a hop and something to run. It earns its cost when many teams share models and need common keys, limits, policy and tracing, not for a single simple caller.

work: Decide your gateway trigger, such as the third team or the second provider, and write it down.
Score candidate gateways on provider coverage, streaming overhead and trace export.
Define the gateway's scope in writing and state that prompts stay with feature teams.

title: Taste first, then watch the tables

beats.say: How does a restaurant know a new recipe is better, both before and after customers taste it?

Before the dish goes on the menu, the chef cooks it for a small panel and compares it with notes from the old recipe. That is an offline eval: a test run on saved examples, before anyone real is affected.

Once it is live, the staff watch the tables. Do plates come back empty? Do people send food back? That is an online eval: watching real customers. You need both, because the panel cannot predict everything.
In AI, the dish is an answer, the panel is a saved question set, and the tables are live users.

check.q: What does an online eval tell you that an offline eval cannot?
opts: How real users respond to answers once the change is live
Whether the saved question set contains any typos in it
Which model has the lowest price per token this month
check.why: Offline evals use saved examples before launch. Only watching live traffic shows how real users behave with the change in place.

work: List which of your AI features have a saved question set and which are only watched after launch.
Write down two live user signals you could already collect, such as retries or thumbs down.

title: Gate the change, then watch the traffic

beats.say: A prompt tweak saves ten percent on cost. Did it quietly make answers worse?

show.sub: You need a way to know

beats.say: First, a golden set: a few hundred real questions with reference answers, refreshed from production. Every prompt edit, model upgrade or retrieval change runs against it in CI. The build fails if the mean score drops more than run-to-run noise, or if any single item drops sharply.

chip.text: Fail on mean drop or sharp item drop

beats.say: Why the item check? A steady average can hide one case that broke badly.

After release, sample live traffic daily. Score thumbs, retries, copied answers and escalations to a person, plus automatic checks like valid JSON, and a judge on a sample. Compare by prompt version, like an A B test.

chip.text: Compare prompt version against prompt version

check.q: A change keeps the mean score flat, but one question goes from correct to badly wrong. What should the gate do?
opts: Fail it, because a sharp single-item drop can hide behind a steady mean
Pass it, because the mean stayed inside the usual run-to-run noise
Pass it, because one item out of hundreds is too small to matter
check.why: A mean can stay steady while one case breaks badly. A good gate checks both the average and individual item drops.

work: Add a per-item drop rule next to the mean-score rule in your CI eval.
Measure run-to-run noise by running the same golden set several times before setting thresholds.

title: Can you trust the judge?

beats.say: Your AI judge agrees with humans seventy percent of the time. Is it good?

Maybe not. If nearly every answer is good, a judge that passes everything also agrees most of the time. So have people label one to two hundred answers, then measure Cohen's kappa, which is agreement beyond chance.
Judges have biases. They like longer answers, favour the first option in a pair, and prefer their own model family. Randomise the order, score against specific criteria, and use a different family.

show.title: Judge biases and fixes
items: Likes longer answers: score set criteria
Likes own family: use a different one

beats.say: Finally, pin the judge's model version and prompt. If the judge changes, last month's scores cannot be compared with this month's.

check.q: A judge agrees with humans 70% of the time, but almost all answers are good. What is the right conclusion?
opts: Agreement may be mostly chance, so check kappa before trusting it
Seventy percent is high enough, so trust it for every release
Agreement is irrelevant, so only the judge's confidence counts
check.why: When most answers are good, a lenient judge agrees often by luck. Kappa removes chance agreement and shows whether the judge adds real signal.

work: Label 100 to 200 answers by hand and compute kappa for your current judge.
Pin judge model version and prompt in config, and log both with every score.

title: Catching confident inventions

beats.say: Your chatbot cites a document, confidently. The document does not exist. How do you catch that?
For answers built on retrieved text, run two checks. Is every cited source really in the retrieved set? And is every claim in the answer supported by that retrieved text?
Track the share of unsupported claims as a metric, per prompt version and model. A rise after a change is your alarm.
Also reward honesty. An answer saying I could not find this beats a confident invention, so your eval set needs questions with no answer in the documents, and should score that refusal as correct.

show.title: Reward honest refusals
items: Score I could not find this as correct

check.q: Which metric best catches confident inventions in a retrieval-based answer?
opts: Share of claims not supported by the retrieved text
Average length of answers across all of the users
Number of documents retrieved for each question
check.why: Invention means claims the retrieved text does not back up. Tracking that share per version shows when a change makes the system invent more.

work: Add an automatic check that every cited source ID appears in the retrieved set.
Add unanswerable questions to the golden set and score a refusal as correct.

title: How much eval is enough?

beats.say: Evals cost money and time. How much checking is enough?

Layer them by price. Cheap automatic checks run on all traffic: valid JSON, citation exists, SQL runs. Judge models cost tokens, so run them on a sample, say one to five percent. Humans label only to calibrate the judge and review disagreements.

Know the limits. A golden set of a few hundred items has noise, so small gains are not provable. It also goes stale as users change, so refresh it from production. And user thumbs are sparse and skewed toward extreme experiences.

show.title: Limits to plan for
items: Few hundred items: small gains are noise
Golden set goes stale: refresh it

beats.say: Choose evals that gate cheaply before release, and monitor continuously after. Spend human time on calibration, not grading everything.

check.q: Where should an architect spend human labelling effort in an eval programme?
opts: Calibrating the judge and reviewing its disagreements
Grading every live answer by hand, so no judge is used
Rewriting the golden set daily so no item ever repeats
check.why: Humans are slow and costly, so use them where they anchor trust in cheaper scorers: calibrating the judge and checking where it disagrees.

work: Draw your eval stack in three layers with a sampling rate and monthly cost for each.
Set a refresh schedule that pulls new real questions into the golden set.

title: A tracking number for one question

beats.say: A customer says their pizza came late and wrong. How do you find out why?
Picture a parcel. It has one tracking number, and every stop is scanned: warehouse, truck, depot, doorstep. When it goes missing, you read the stops in order.
A trace is that tracking number for one question to an AI app. Each step, like looking up documents or asking the model, is a span. That means one scanned stop, with its time and cost.

chip.text: Each span has time and cost

beats.say: Now a slow answer is easy to explain. Maybe the lookup took four seconds. Without a trace, you only have piles of separate logs and a guess.

check.q: What is a span in a trace?
opts: One recorded step of a request, with its time and details
A summary of all requests for a whole day
A copy of the final answer the user received
A rule that blocks slow requests from running
check.why: A trace covers one request, and each span is one step inside it, like a single scanned stop on a parcel's journey.

work: Pick one slow or wrong answer from a user and list every step it went through.
Ask your team whether you can look up one request by a single ID today.

title: Anatomy of a trace and its spans

beats.say: One user request touches five systems. How do you see all of it?

show.sub: One trace ID ties them together

beats.say: You give the request one trace ID. Each step becomes a span: retrieval, the model call, a tool call, a retry. Spans nest under the trace, in order, with start and end times.
Each model span records the model version, prompt template version, input, cached and output tokens, cost, time to first token, and finish reason.

show.title: Inside a model span
items: Cost and time to first token

beats.say: Say retrieval took 200 milliseconds, the model took 6 seconds, and the finish reason was length limit. Now you know the answer was cut off, and exactly which step was slow.
OpenTelemetry names these attributes, so any backend can read them.

check.q: A trace shows a 6 second model span that ended with finish reason length limit. What does that tell you?
opts: The model call was slow and the answer was cut off
The retrieval step returned the wrong documents
The cache was hit and the answer was reused
The user cancelled the request before it finished
check.why: Finish reason length limit means the output stopped at the token cap, and the span time shows the model call was the slow step.

work: Add prompt template version and token counts to every model span.
Record finish reason, and review requests that ended on length limit.

title: Privacy and the spans that find root causes

beats.say: Your traces now hold every user's private text. Is that a problem?
Yes. Prompts contain names, emails, and sometimes medical details. Redact personal data before it is stored, not after.
Keep prompt bodies for days, not years, and limit who can read them. Numbers like tokens, cost and latency hold no secrets, so keep those for months.
Also record what retrieval returned, and tool arguments with success or failure. A wrong answer is often a wrong document, not a bad model. Without that span, you would blame the wrong thing.

check.q: How should you set retention for trace data in an LLM system?
opts: Keep prompt text briefly and the numbers much longer
Keep prompt text forever so you can always replay it
Delete all numbers fast and keep only the prompt text
Keep everything the same length to stay consistent
check.why: Prompt bodies hold personal text so they should expire in days, while tokens, cost and latency are safe and useful for long trends.

work: Add a redaction step before spans are written to storage.
Set short expiry on prompt bodies and restrict who can read them.

title: From traces to dashboards and alerts

beats.say: At 3 a.m., an agent loops and burns two thousand dollars. What would have caught it?

show.sub: An agent stuck in a loop

beats.say: Roll spans up per feature: requests, p95 time to first token, cost per request, error and fallback rates, cache hit rate, and the latest eval score.

show.title: Per feature dashboard
items: Requests and p95 time to first token
Cost per request and per day
Cache hit rate and eval score

beats.say: Alert on three things. A cost spike, which means a loop or a prompt that doubled. A rising fallback rate, which means a provider is struggling. A falling eval score after a model update.
Tag every span with team and feature, or cost reports cannot be split. And link every alert to example traces, so the on-call person starts with evidence, not guesses.

show.title: Make alerts useful
items: Tag team and feature on every span
Link each alert to example traces

check.q: Your daily cost doubles overnight and no code shipped. What does the setup need most to find the cause fast?
opts: Cost per feature with alert links to example traces
One total monthly bill compared with last month
A weekly report of average latency for all calls
Full prompt text kept for every request for years
check.why: Cost broken down by feature, with the alert linking to real traces, shows which feature changed and why, such as a loop or a bigger prompt.

work: Tag every model span with team and feature so costs can be split.
Create cost, fallback and eval score alerts that link to example traces.
Review the dashboard after every model or prompt change.
